<!-- thm--1: body_md -->
Under mild hypotheses, the zero-mode partition function $Z_{\mathbb H(X;\mathcal{F})}(L)$ is independent of the choice of maximal admissible Lagrangian $L$.
<!-- end thm--1 -->
<!-- defn-1: body_md -->
A \emph{$(-1)$-shifted symplectic pairing} on $V$ is a nondegenerate graded skew-symmetric pairing
	\[
	\omega \colon V \times V \longrightarrow \mathbb{R}[-1].
	\]
	
	Graded skew-symmetry means that $\omega(V^k,V^\ell)=0$ unless $k+\ell=1$, and
	\[
	\omega(x,y)=-(-1)^{(k-1)(\ell-1)}\omega(y,x).
	\]
	for $x \in V^k$ and $y \in V^\ell$. 
	
	Nondegeneracy means that the map
	\[
	\omega^\flat \colon V \xlongrightarrow{\sim} V^\vee[-1],
	\qquad x\longmapsto\omega(x,-),
	\]
	is an isomorphism.
<!-- end defn-1 -->
<!-- defn-2: body_md -->
A (graded) lattice $\Gamma \subset V$ is called \emph{integral} if
	\[
	\omega(\Gamma,\Gamma)\subset\mathbb{Z}.
	\]
	It is called \emph{full} if
	\[
	\Gamma_\mathbb{R} \coloneqq  \Gamma\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}}\mathbb{R} \cong V.
	\]
    Its \emph{radical} is
	\[
	\mathrm{rad}(\Gamma)\coloneq\{\gamma\in\Gamma\mid \omega(\gamma,\Gamma)=0\}.
	\]
<!-- end defn-2 -->
<!-- defn-3: body_md -->
A complex \emph{quadratic weight} on $A$ is a map
\[
w:A\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}/i\mathbb{Z}
\]
such that
\begin{itemize}
	\item $w(x+y)-w(x)-w(y)$ is biadditive;
	\item $\Re\bigl(w(x)\bigr)=\Re\bigl(w(-x)\bigr)$.
\end{itemize}
<!-- end defn-3 -->
<!-- lem-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:real-quadratic}
The function $q$ vanishes on $\mathrm{Tor}(A)$ and descends uniquely to a real quadratic weight
\[
\bar q:A_{\mathrm{free}}\coloneq A/\mathrm{Tor}(A)\longrightarrow\mathbb{R}
\]
satisfying $\bar q(nx)=n^2\bar q(x)$ for every $n\in\mathbb{Z}$.
<!-- end lem-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Let $b(x,y)\coloneqq q(x+y)-q(x)-q(y)$. Since $q(-x)=q(x)$, the identity $0=q(x-x)=2q(x)-b(x,x)$ gives $b(x,x)=2q(x)$. Since $2 \in \mathbb{R}$ is invertible, $q(nx)= b(nx,nx)/2=n^2q(x)$. If $t$ is torsion and $nt=0$, then $0=q(nt)=n^2q(t)$, so $q(t)=0$. Moreover $n b(x,t)=b(x,nt)=0$, and therefore $b(x,t)=0$. Thus $q(x+t)=q(x)$, proving that $q$ descends to $A_{\mathrm{free}}$.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- defn-4: body_md -->
\label{def:abelian-BV-group}
A \emph{BV structure} on $H$ is a triple $(\omega,\kappa,w)$, where:
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2em]
\item $\omega$ is a $(-1)$-shifted symplectic pairing on $\mathfrak{h}$;
\item $\kappa = \bigoplus \kappa^k$ is a direct sum of inner products $\kappa^k$ on $\mathfrak{h}^k$ for which
\[
\omega^\flat:(\mathfrak{h},\kappa)\xlongrightarrow{\sim}(\mathfrak{h}^\vee[-1],\kappa^\vee[-1])
\]
is an isometry;
\item $w$ is a complex quadratic weight on $\pi_0(H^0)$. 
\end{itemize}
We call $H$, equipped with such a BV structure, an \emph{abelian BV group}.
<!-- end defn-4 -->
<!-- defn-5: body_md -->
A \emph{Lagrangian} of $H$ is a family of closed subgroups
	\[
	L=\{L^k\subset H^k\}_{k\in\mathbb{Z}}
	\]
	such that the total Lie algebra $\mathfrak{l}\subset\mathfrak{h}$ is Lagrangian and the induced map
	\[
	\pi_0(L^k)\longrightarrow\pi_0(H^k)
	\]
	is injective for all $k\in\mathbb{Z}$.
<!-- end defn-5 -->
<!-- lem-2: body_md -->
Every integrable abelian BV group $H$ has an admissible Lagrangian.
<!-- end lem-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
Choose a Lagrangian subspace $\underline{\mathfrak{l}}$ of the reduced symplectic space $\Gamma_\mathbb{R}/\mathrm{rad}(\Gamma)_\mathbb{R}$ rational with respect to $\underline\Gamma = \Gamma/\mathrm{rad}(\Gamma)$, and let $\mathfrak{l} \subset\Gamma_\mathbb{R}$ be its inverse
	image. Then $\mathfrak{l}$ is Lagrangian in $\mathfrak{h}$ and $\Gamma\cap\mathfrak{l}$ is a full lattice
	in $\mathfrak{l}$. Hence
	\[
	L \coloneq \exp(\mathfrak{l})\subset H_0
	\]
	is a compact connected Lagrangian. In particular, $\pi_0(L)=0$, so $L$ is admissible.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- lem-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:integrable-admissible}
	A Lagrangian $L$ is admissible if and only if
	\[
	\int_{L^{\mathrm{even}}} \left|\exp(-2\pi w)\right|\,\mu_{\mathrm{even}}<\infty,
	\qquad
	\int_{L^{\mathrm{odd}}}1\ \mu_{\mathrm{odd}}<\infty,
	\]
	where $\mu_{\mathrm{even}}$ and $\mu_{\mathrm{odd}}$ denote the positive densities on $L^{\mathrm{even}}$ and $L^{\mathrm{odd}}$ induced by $\kappa$.
<!-- end lem-3 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
Since $|\exp(-2\pi w)|=\exp(-2\pi\Re(w))$ is constant on connected components and $\mu_{\mathrm{even}}$ is translation-invariant,
	\[
	\int_{L^{\mathrm{even}}} \left|\exp(-2\pi w)\right|\,\mu_{\mathrm{even}}
	=
	\mathrm{vol}(L^{\mathrm{even}}_0)
	|\pi_0(L^{\mathrm{even}})/\pi_0(L^0)|
	\sum_{c\in\pi_0(L^0)}\exp(-2\pi\Re(w(c))).
	\]
	The volume factor is finite precisely when $L^{\mathrm{even}}_0$ is compact. The second factor is finite precisely when $\pi_0(L^{\mathrm{even}})/\pi_0(L^0)$ is finite. By Lemma~\ref{lem:real-quadratic}, the series is a finite torsion factor times a Gaussian sum over the free lattice. It converges if and only if the induced real quadratic form is positive definite.
		
	Likewise,
	\[
	\int_{L^{\mathrm{odd}}}1\ \mu_{\mathrm{odd}} = |\pi_0(L^{\mathrm{odd}})|
	\mathrm{vol}(L^{\mathrm{odd}}_0),
	\]
	which is finite precisely when the identity component $L^{\mathrm{odd}}_0$ is compact and the component group $\pi_0(L^{\mathrm{odd}})$ is finite.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- defn-6: body_md -->
For a maximal admissible Lagrangian $L$, define
\begin{equation}\label{eq:BV-partition}
Z_H(L)\coloneq
\frac{\displaystyle\int_{L^{\mathrm{even}}}\exp(- 2\pi w)\,\mu_{\mathrm{even}}}
{\displaystyle\int_{L^{\mathrm{odd}}}1\ \mu_{\mathrm{odd}}}.
\end{equation}
We call $Z_H(L)$ the \emph{zero-mode partition function} of $H$ (with respect to $L$).
<!-- end defn-6 -->
<!-- prop-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:partition-factorization}
For every maximal admissible Lagrangian $L$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:partition-factorization}
Z_H(L)=\mathrm{vol}(L_0)\, T(H)\, \Theta(L).
\end{equation}
<!-- end prop-1 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
Enlarging a Lagrangian by discrete components does not change its Lie algebra. Maximality therefore forces
\[
\pi_0(L^k)=
\mathrm{Tor}(\pi_0(H^k)), \qquad k\ne0.
\]
The rest follows from the proof of Lemma \ref{lem:integrable-admissible}.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- lem-4: body_md -->
\label{lem:unimodular-volume}
Suppose that $\Gamma$ is a full unimodular lattice in $\mathfrak{h}$, and let $\mathfrak{l}\subset\mathfrak{h}$ be a Lagrangian such that 
\[
\Gamma_L\coloneq\Gamma\cap\mathfrak{l}
\]
is full in $\mathfrak{l}$. Then
\[
\mathrm{vol}(L_0)=\bigl({\det}_\Gamma \kappa \bigr)^{1/4},
\qquad
{\det}_\Gamma \kappa \coloneq\prod_k\bigl({\det}_{\Gamma^k}\kappa^k\bigr)^{(-1)^k}.
\]
In particular, the graded volume $\mathrm{vol}(L_0)$ is independent of the embedding $L_0\hookrightarrow H_0$.
<!-- end lem-4 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
Unimodularity and the Lagrangian condition give an exact sequence of graded lattices
\[
0\longrightarrow\Gamma_L\longrightarrow\Gamma
\longrightarrow\Gamma_L^\vee[-1]\longrightarrow0.
\]
Taking Berezinian lines yields
\[
\mathrm{Ber}_\mathbb{Z}(\Gamma)\cong
\mathrm{Ber}_\mathbb{Z}(\Gamma_L)\otimes\mathrm{Ber}_\mathbb{Z}(\Gamma_L^\vee[-1])
\cong\mathrm{Ber}_\mathbb{Z}(\Gamma_L)^{\otimes2}.
\]
Compatibility of $\kappa$ and $\omega$ makes this identification an isometry. Taking norms of the integral Berezinian generators $1_\Gamma \in \mathrm{Ber}_\mathbb{Z}(\Gamma)$ and $1_{\Gamma_L} \in \mathrm{Ber}_\mathbb{Z}(\Gamma_L)$ then gives
\[
({\det}_{\Gamma}\kappa)^{1/2}
=\lVert 1_{\Gamma}\rVert
=\lVert 1_{\Gamma_L}\rVert^2
={\det}_{\Gamma_L}\kappa|_{\Gamma_L}
=\mathrm{vol}_{\kappa}(L_0)^2.
\]
and the result follows.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- thm-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:L-independence}
The zero-mode partition function $Z_H(L)$ of a nice $H$ is independent of the maximal admissible Lagrangian $L$.
<!-- end thm-1 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
By Proposition~\ref{prop:partition-factorization}, $Z_H(L)=\mathrm{vol}(L_0)\, T(H)\, \Theta(L)$. The torsion factor $T(H)$ is independent of $L$. Since $H$ is nice, $q=\Re(w)$ is positive definite on the real span of the free part of $\pi_0(H^0)$. Maximality therefore forces
\[
\pi_0(L^0)=\pi_0(H^0).
\]
Hence $\Theta(L)$ is also independent of $L$. 

It remains only to prove that $\mathrm{vol}(L_0)$ is independent of $L$. 
Since $L_0$ is compact, its Lie algebra satisfies $\mathfrak{l}\subset\Gamma_\mathbb{R}$. As $\Gamma_\mathbb{R}^{\perp_\omega} \subset \Gamma_\mathbb{R}$ and $\mathfrak{l}$ is Lagrangian,
\[
\Gamma_\mathbb{R}^{\perp_\omega} \subset \mathfrak{l}^{\perp_\omega}=\mathfrak{l}.
\]
Consequently $\Gamma\cap \Gamma_\mathbb{R}^{\perp_\omega} \subset\Gamma_L=\Gamma\cap\mathfrak{l}$. Coisotropic reduction then gives an inclusion of lattices
\[
\underline\Gamma_L \coloneq \Gamma_L/(\Gamma\cap \Gamma_\mathbb{R}^{\perp_\omega} )
\subset
\underline\Gamma = \Gamma/\mathrm{rad}(\Gamma).
\]
The latter is unimodular by assumption. Equip $\Gamma_\mathbb{R}^{\perp_\omega}$ and $\underline{\Gamma}_\mathbb{R} = \Gamma_\mathbb{R}/\Gamma_\mathbb{R}^{\perp_\omega}$ with the inner products induced by $\kappa$. Graded covolumes are multiplicative for the resulting short exact sequence of lattices
\[
0 \longrightarrow \Gamma\cap \Gamma_\mathbb{R}^{\perp_\omega} \longrightarrow \Gamma_L \longrightarrow \underline\Gamma_L \longrightarrow 0,
\]
which is full in the short exact sequence of Euclidean vector spaces
\[
0 \longrightarrow \Gamma_\mathbb{R}^{\perp_\omega} \longrightarrow (\Gamma_L)_\mathbb{R} = \mathfrak{l} \longrightarrow (\underline \Gamma_L)_\mathbb{R} \longrightarrow 0.
\]
It follows that
\[
\mathrm{vol}(L_0)
=
\mathrm{covol}(\Gamma_L)
=
\mathrm{covol}(\Gamma \cap \Gamma_\mathbb{R}^{\perp_\omega})\,
\mathrm{covol}(\underline\Gamma_L).
\]
The first factor is manifestly independent of $L$, while Lemma~\ref{lem:unimodular-volume} implies that the second factor is also independent of $L$.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- defn-7: body_md -->
We call $\mathcal{E}_S$ the \emph{equation-of-motion} map of $S$, and say that $S$ is \emph{local} if there exists a morphism of complexes
	\[
	K\colon \mathrm{Bund}_\nabla(p+1)
	\longrightarrow
	\Omega_{\mathrm{cl}}^{n-p}
	\]
	such that the induced map on zeroth hypercohomology agrees with $\mathcal{E}_S$.
<!-- end defn-7 -->
<!-- lem-5: body_md -->
\label{selfdual}
	$K$ satisfies
	\[
	\int_X  K \alpha \wedge \beta = (-1)^{p(n-p)} \int_X \alpha \wedge K \beta.
	\]
<!-- end lem-5 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
This follows from the computation
	\[
	\frac{\partial^2}{\partial s \partial t} \bigg|_{s=t=0} S(s \beta + t\alpha) = \epsilon_S \int_X \alpha \wedge \mathcal{E}_S(\beta) = \epsilon_S \int_X \alpha \wedge K \beta
	\]
	and the symmetry of partial derivatives.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- lem-6: body_md -->
We have
	\[
	\Omega^p_{\mathrm{cl}}(X)\subseteq \ker K,
	\qquad
	\operatorname{im}K\subseteq \Omega^{n-p}_{\mathrm{ex}}(X).
	\]
	Using harmonic representatives with respect to $g$, there are injections
	\[
	H^p_{\mathrm{dR}}(X)
	\hookrightarrow
	H^0\!\bigl(\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{pert}}(X)\bigr),
	\qquad
	H^{n-p}_{\mathrm{dR}}(X)
	\hookrightarrow
	H^1\!\bigl(\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{pert}}(X)\bigr).
	\]
<!-- end lem-6 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
The first inclusion follows directly from the Poincar\'e lemma: every global closed $p$-form is locally exact and hence lies in the kernel of $K$. The second inclusion follows from Lemma \ref{selfdual} and Poincar\'e duality.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- defn-8: body_md -->
We call $S$ \emph{elliptic} if $\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{pert}}(X)$ is an elliptic complex.
<!-- end defn-8 -->
<!-- lem-7: body_md -->
\label{star}
	The Hodge star operator
	\[
	\star: H_D^k(X) \xlongrightarrow{\sim} H_D^{1-k}(X)
	\]
	defines an isometry of inner product spaces.
<!-- end lem-7 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
By Lemma \ref{selfdual}, $D$ satisfies
	\[
	\int_X D \alpha \wedge \beta = \pm \int_X \alpha \wedge D \beta.
	\]
	It follows that
	\[
	D^*=\pm \star D\star.
	\]
	Hence $H_D(X)=\ker D\cap\ker(D\star)$ and $H_D(X)$ is preserved by $\star$. Since $\star^2=\pm 1$, the Hodge star restricts to an isomorphism on $H_D(X)$. Moreover, it is an isometry with respect to the inner product:
	$
	\langle \star\alpha_h,\star\beta_h\rangle_g
	=
	\langle \alpha_h,\beta_h\rangle_g.
	$
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- prop-2: body_md -->
The finite-dimensional graded vector space $H\bigl(\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{pert}}(X)\bigr)$ carries a canonical $(-1)$-shifted symplectic pairing
	\[
	\omega\colon
	H^k\!\bigl(\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{pert}}(X)\bigr)
	\times
	H^{1-k}\!\bigl(\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{pert}}(X)\bigr)
	\longrightarrow \mathbb{R},
	\]
	given by
	\[
	\omega([\alpha],[\beta])
	=
	\begin{cases}
		\displaystyle \int_X \alpha_h\wedge\beta_h, & k\leq 0,\\[6pt]
		\displaystyle -\int_X \beta_h\wedge\alpha_h, & k>0,
	\end{cases}
	\]
	where $\alpha_h$ and $\beta_h$ denote the harmonic representatives of
	$[\alpha]$ and $[\beta]$, respectively.
	
	Moreover, $\omega$ is compatible with the inner product
	\[
	\kappa\colon
	H^k\!\bigl(\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{pert}}(X)\bigr)
	\times
	H^k\!\bigl(\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{pert}}(X)\bigr)
	\longrightarrow \mathbb{R},
	\qquad
	\kappa([\alpha],[\beta])
	=
	\langle \alpha_h,\beta_h\rangle_g
	=
	\int_X \alpha_h\wedge\star\beta_h.
	\]
<!-- end prop-2 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
Nondegeneracy of $\omega$ follows from the Hodge decomposition. More precisely,
	if $\alpha_h\in H_D(X)$, then
	\[
	\int_X \alpha_h\wedge\bigl(D\gamma\pm\star D\star\eta\bigr)
	=
	\pm\int_X \star\alpha_h\wedge D\star\eta
	=
	\pm\int_X D\star\alpha_h\wedge\star\eta
	=
	0.
	\]
	Thus $H_D(X)$ is orthogonal, with respect to the Poincar\'e pairing, to the non-harmonic summands in the Hodge decomposition. Since the Poincar\'e pairing on differential forms is nondegenerate, its restriction to $H_D(X)$ is therefore nondegenerate.
	
	To see that $\omega$ is compatible with $\kappa$, observe that
	\[
	\omega^\flat=\pm \kappa^\flat \circ \star.
	\]
	By Lemma \ref{star}, the Hodge star is an isometry, and hence $\omega^\flat$ is an isometry.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- lem-8: body_md -->
\label{lem:master-hypercohomology}
	For every $k$, there is a natural exact sequence of abelian groups
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:master-hypercohomology}
		0
		\longrightarrow \operatorname{im}(\delta^k)
		\longrightarrow H^k\bigl(\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{pert}}(X)\bigr)
		\longrightarrow \mathbb H^k(X;\mathcal{F})
		\longrightarrow \ker(\delta^{k+1})
		\longrightarrow 0.
	\end{equation}
	In particular, $\mathbb H^k(X;\mathcal{F})$ is canonically an abelian Lie group with
	Lie algebra
	\[
	H^k\bigl(\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{pert}}(X)\bigr),
	\]
	exponential lattice
	\[
	\operatorname{im}(\delta^k)
	\subset H^k\bigl(\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{pert}}(X)\bigr),
	\]
	and group of connected components
	\[
	\ker(\delta^{k+1})
	\subset H^{k+p+1}(X;\mathbb{Z}).
	\]
<!-- end lem-8 -->
<!-- lem-9: body_md -->
The function $S_{\mathrm{crit}}$ is constant on every connected component of $\mathbb H^0(X;\mathcal{F})$ and vanishes on the identity component. Thus, it descends to a complex quadratic weight
	\[
	w \colon \pi_0 \bigl(\mathbb H^0(X;\mathcal{F})\bigr)
	\longrightarrow \mathbb{C}/i\mathbb{Z}.
	\]
<!-- end lem-9 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
The identity component of $\mathbb H^0(X;\mathcal{F})$ is the image of
	\[
	\exp\colon
	H^0(\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{pert}}(X))
	=
	\frac{\ker K}{\Omega_{\mathrm{ex}}^p(X)}
	\longrightarrow
	\mathbb H^0(X;\mathcal{F}).
	\]
	Let $x\in\mathbb H^0(X;\mathcal{F})$ and $[\alpha]\in H^0(\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{pert}}(X))$, with harmonic representative $\alpha_h$. The path
	\[
	t\longmapsto x+\exp(t[\alpha])
	\]
	lies in the same connected component of the critical locus. Writing $\check A=\mathbb H^0(\mathrm{For})(x)$, linearity of the equation-of-motion map gives
	\[
	\mathcal{E}_S(\check A+t\alpha_h)=\mathcal{E}_S(\check A)+tK\alpha_h = \mathbb H^0(K)(\check A) = 0,
	\]
	where we use $K \alpha_h = 0$ and $\mathbb H^0(K) \circ\mathbb H^0(\mathrm{For}) = 0$. It follows that
	\[
	\frac{d}{dt}S_{\mathrm{crit}}\bigl(x+\exp(t[\alpha])\bigr)
	=\epsilon_S\int_X\alpha_h\wedge\mathcal{E}_S(\check A+t\alpha_h) = 0.
	\]
	Thus $S_{\mathrm{crit}}$ is constant on every connected component. On the identity component this constant is $S(0)=0$.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- thm-2: body_md -->
The data $(\omega,\kappa,w)$ defined above endow the collection of abelian Lie groups $\mathbb H^\bullet(X;\mathcal{F})$ with the structure of an abelian BV group.
<!-- end thm-2 -->
<!-- lem-10: body_md -->
The perturbative hypercohomology is
\[
H^k(\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm M, \mathrm{pert}}(X)) =
\begin{cases}
H^{p+k}_{\mathrm{dR}}(X),&k \leq 0,\\
H^{n-p+k-1}_{\mathrm{dR}}(X),&k >0.
\end{cases}
\]
Under these identifications,
\[
\delta^k=
\begin{cases}
\rho^{p+k},&k\le0,\\
0,&k>0,
\end{cases}
\]
<!-- end lem-10 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
Away from the middle arrow, the perturbative BV complex is the de Rham complex. At degree zero,
\[
H^0(\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm M, \mathrm{pert}}(X))
=\ker K_{\mathrm M}/\Omega^p_{\mathrm{ex}}(X).
\]
For the Maxwell operator, Hodge decomposition gives $\ker K_{\mathrm M}=\Omega^p_{\mathrm{cl}}(X)$ and $\operatorname{im} K_{\mathrm M} = \Omega^{n-p}_{\mathrm{ex}}(X)$; hence
\[
H^0(\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm M, \mathrm{pert}}(X))= H^p_{\mathrm{dR}}(X), \qquad H^1(\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm M, \mathrm{pert}}(X))= H^{n-p}_{\mathrm{dR}}(X).
\]

For $k \leq 0$, the connecting map is induced by $\mathbb{Z}\hookrightarrow\mathbb{R}$ and is therefore the usual integral-to-de Rham map. For $k > 0$, a topological class contributes through the curvature, but the equation-of-motion term is $d \star F$ and is exact; its cohomology class is therefore zero.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- rmk-1: body_md -->
Therefore, for $j<0$ there is a natural short exact sequence
	\[
	0\longrightarrow
	\frac{\mathcal H^{p+j}}{\Lambda^{p+j}}
	\longrightarrow
	\mathbb{H}^j(X;\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm M})
	\longrightarrow
	\mathrm{Tor}(H^{p+j+1}(X;\mathbb{Z}))
	\longrightarrow 0,
	\]
	while in degree zero,
	\[
	0\longrightarrow
	\frac{\mathcal H^p}{\Lambda^p}
	\longrightarrow
	\mathbb{H}^0(X;\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm M})
	\longrightarrow
	H^{p+1}(X;\mathbb{Z})
	\longrightarrow 0.
	\]
	For $j>0$, one has
	\[
	0\longrightarrow
	\mathcal H^{n-p+j-1}
	\longrightarrow
	\mathbb{H}^j(X;\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm M})
	\longrightarrow
	H^{p+j+1}(X;\mathbb{Z})
	\longrightarrow 0.
	\]
<!-- end rmk-1 -->
<!-- prop-3: body_md -->
The abelian BV group $H_{\mathrm M}$ is nice.
<!-- end prop-3 -->
<!-- rmk-2: body_md -->
\label{rmk:maxwell-comparison}
	Compared with the zero-mode contribution to the higher Maxwell partition function obtained in \cite[Eq.~(22)]{DonnellyMichelWall} and \cite[Eq.~(47.21)]{MooreSaxena}, \eqref{eq:maxwell-partition} contains a different torsion factor. This difference arises essentially from the presence of antifields in the BV complex together with the maximality requirement on the gauge-fixing Lagrangian $L$.
<!-- end rmk-2 -->
<!-- lem-11: body_md -->
\label{lem:CS-cohomology}
The perturbative hypercohomology and connecting maps are
\[
H^j(\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{CS},\mathrm{pert}}(X))\cong H^{p+j}_{\mathrm{dR}}(X),
\qquad
\delta^j=a_j\rho^{p+j},
\qquad
a_j=\begin{cases}1,&j\le0,\\ k,&j>0.\end{cases}
\]
<!-- end lem-11 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
The perturbative complex differs from the de Rham complex only by multiplying its middle differential by the nonzero scalar $k$, so its cohomology is unchanged. The connecting map is the integral-to-de Rham map before the middle arrow and acquires one factor of $k$ after crossing it.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- prop-4: body_md -->
$H_{\mathrm{CS}}$ is integrable, and is nice precisely for $k=\pm1$.
<!-- end prop-4 -->
<!-- lem-12: body_md -->
\label{lem:MCS-cohomology}
The perturbative cohomology agrees with that of Chern--Simons theory away from the middle degrees, while
\[
H^0(\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{MCS},\mathrm{pert}}(X))
\cong H^p_{\mathrm{dR}}(X)\oplus R_{e,k},
\qquad
H^1(\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{MCS},\mathrm{pert}}(X))
\cong H^{p+1}_{\mathrm{dR}}(X)\oplus dR_{e,k}.
\]
<!-- end lem-12 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
Under the Hodge decomposition
$\Omega^p=\mathcal H^p\oplus\Omega^p_{\mathrm{ex}}\oplus\Omega^p_{\mathrm{coex}}$,
the middle differential vanishes on the first two summands and equals $d(e^{-2}\star d+k)$ on the last. Since $d$ is injective on coexact forms,
\[
\ker K_{\mathrm{MCS}}=\Omega^p_{\mathrm{cl}}\oplus R_{e,k}.
\]
Self-adjointness gives $\Omega^p_{\mathrm{coex}}=R_{e,k}\oplus\operatorname{im}(e^{-2}\star d+k)$; applying $d$ and taking the quotient in degree one gives the second formula.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- prop-5: body_md -->
If $R_{e,k}=0$, then
	\begin{equation*}                         
		Z_{H_{\mathrm{MCS}}}(L)=Z_{H_{\mathrm{CS}}}(L),
	\end{equation*}
	with the right-hand side given by \eqref{eq:CS-partition}.
<!-- end prop-5 -->
